title: Left-sided weakness after a fall from standing

source.citation: Baldwin ML, Shufflebarger EF, Pacheco ZS. Chalk-Stick Fracture in Ankylosing Spondylitis: A Case Report of Cervical Spine Injury Following Minor Trauma. Cureus. 2024;16(9):e68931.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Sudden left-sided weakness and neck pain after a fall from standing
presentation.hpi: Known ankylosing spondylitis and a stable left cerebellopontine angle meningioma. He fell from standing and hit his head, without loss of consciousness, and then developed abrupt left-sided weakness and neck pain; he can no longer stand or walk on his own. He denies numbness, tingling and bowel or bladder incontinence. Paramedics called a prehospital stroke alert, and he arrives in a cervical collar.

exam: Alert and oriented; severe neck pain
Cervical collar in place; midline cervical tenderness without step-off, deformity, abrasion or laceration
Pupils equal and reactive, eye movements full, face symmetric, speech clear
Power 2/5 in the left arm and leg, 4/5 on the right
Hoffmann sign positive; Babinski upgoing bilaterally; reflexes 2+ and symmetric
Baseline profound hearing loss limits coordination and pronator drift testing

imaging.modality: Non-contrast CT, CT angiography and CT perfusion of head and neck (stroke alert)
imaging.finding: Known cerebellopontine angle meningioma; no acute infarct or penumbra
Ankylosed spine with a fracture through the C6–C7 disc involving the C7 superior endplate and posteroinferior C6; 75% anterolisthesis of C6 on C7; posterior epidural haematoma
Chalk-stick fracture through C5–C7 with grade 2 traumatic anterolisthesis of C6 on C7; epidural haemorrhage extending from C5 into the thoracic spine

diagnosis.primary: Unstable C5–C7 chalk-stick fracture in ankylosing spondylitis with traumatic C6–C7 anterolisthesis, spinal epidural haematoma and cervical cord injury, after a fall from standing
differentials: Central cord syndrome from hyperextension on a stenotic spine
Todd paresis after an unwitnessed seizure

management: Prehospital stroke alert: non-contrast CT, CT angiography and CT perfusion
CT cervical spine; orthopaedic and trauma surgery consulted
Posterior cervical decompression and fusion C3–T3, completed over two days because of intraoperative haemodynamic instability
Intubated in the trauma and burn ICU; extubated 3 days later
Oropharyngeal dysphagia: Dobhoff feeding tube, then percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy
outcome: Discharged home 2 months after the injury, after a month of inpatient rehabilitation, with persistent left-sided weakness and PEG feeding; weakness improving at follow-up one month later.
teachingPoints: In ankylosing spondylitis the fused, osteoporotic spine breaks like a long bone: low-energy falls cause transverse, three-column (chalk-stick) fractures, most often at C6–C7, that are usually unstable.
NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule do not address or explicitly exclude ankylosing spondylitis: image every such patient with neck pain after trauma by CT, with a low threshold for MRI.

New neurological deficit after a fall in AS means spinal cord injury or epidural haematoma until proven otherwise, even when a stroke alert has been called; bilateral upper motor neuron signs with neck pain localise to the cervical cord.
Immobilise in the pre-injury (often kyphotic) alignment; forcing the neck straight into a standard collar can displace the fracture.
Instability, epidural haematoma or a deteriorating examination need urgent spinal surgery; haematomas can also appear hours after injury.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of his weakness?
questions.extra: Non-contrast CT, CT angiography and CT perfusion of the head: known meningioma; no acute infarct or penumbra.
options: Right middle cerebral artery stroke not yet visible on CT
Unstable cervical spine fracture with cord compression
Todd paresis after an unwitnessed seizure causing the fall
Acute haemorrhage into the cerebellopontine angle meningioma
questions.explanation: Severe midline neck pain after a fall, weakness on both sides (left 2/5, right 4/5) and bilateral upper motor neuron signs (Hoffmann, Babinski) localise to the cervical cord, not one hemisphere. In ankylosing spondylitis the rigid, osteoporotic spine fractures after low-energy falls, so a negative stroke work-up should prompt cervical spine imaging.

questions.q: Which cervical spine imaging strategy is most appropriate?
options: Three-view radiographs first, with CT only if they are abnormal
No imaging if he passes the Canadian C-spine rule once calm
CT of the cervical spine, plus MRI for the cord and canal
Flexion–extension radiographs to look for instability
questions.explanation: NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule do not address or explicitly exclude ankylosing spondylitis, so these patients need CT after any trauma; MRI then shows cord compression, ligamentous injury and epidural haematoma (here from C5 into the thoracic spine). Radiographs miss fractures through the fused, osteopenic spine, and flexion–extension views are dangerous.

questions.q: While awaiting surgery, how should his neck be immobilised?
questions.extra: CT cervical spine: fracture through the C6–C7 disc with 75% anterolisthesis of C6 on C7 and a posterior epidural haematoma.
options: In his pre-injury alignment with padding, without forcing it straight
In a rigid collar after bringing the neck into neutral alignment
With cervical traction weights applied in the emergency department
Not at all, because a fused spine remains inherently stable
questions.explanation: The ankylosed cervical spine is usually kyphotic; straightening it into a standard collar can displace the fracture and worsen cord injury. Immobilise in the patient's pre-injury posture with padding and blocks, and involve spinal surgery early: instability and epidural haematoma required decompression and C3–T3 fusion here.

evidence.quote: A 74-year-old male with a history of AS and stable left cerebellopontine angle meningioma
abrupt left-sided weakness and neck pain following a fall from standing
He had new difficulty ambulating due to this weakness and was unable to stand or walk on his own.
The patient endorsed hitting his head but denied loss of consciousness. He also denied numbness, tingling, bowel incontinence, or bladder incontinence.
the patient was alert and oriented but reported severe neck pain
heart rate of 110 beats per minute and blood pressure of 167/104 mm/Hg. His respiratory rate was 18 respirations per minute
his oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 95% on room air. He had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15.
A cervical collar was in place on arrival, and the patient had tenderness to palpation over the cervical spine without any appreciable step-offs, deformities, abrasions, or lacerations.
pupils were equally round and reactive, external ocular movements intact, and gaze conjugate. His face was symmetric with intact strength and sensation, and his speech was clear
His strength was 2/5 in the left upper and lower extremities and 4/5 on the right.
Hoffman’s sign was positive, and he had upgoing Babinski’s bilaterally. Reflexes were 2+ and symmetric throughout.
He had profound hearing loss at baseline that limited evaluation of coordination and pronator drift commands.
A stroke alert was initiated pre-hospital, and the patient received non-contrasted computed tomography (CT) imaging, as well as CT angiography and CT perfusion scans
These studies showed his known cerebellopontine angle mass without signs of acute cerebral infarct or penumbra.
revealed ankylosis of the spine, as well as a fracture through the C6-C7 disc
with involvement of the superior endplate of the C7 vertebra and right posterior inferior aspect of the C6 vertebra
There was also 75% anterolisthesis of C6 on C7 and a posterior epidural hematoma.
Given these findings, orthopedic surgery and trauma surgery services were consulted.
confirmed a chalk-stick fracture of C5, C6, and C7 vertebrae with grade 2 traumatic anterolisthesis of C6 on C7
an epidural hemorrhage extending from C5 to the thoracic spine was again visualized
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his cervical spine revealed a chalk-stick fracture of C5-C7, which required surgical intervention
mild hyperglycemia (123 mg/dL), elevated creatine kinase (291 units/L), and leukocytosis (21.54 x 10³ WBC with 91% neutrophils)
Prothrombin time (PT) was slightly elevated at 14.7 seconds. The international normalized ratio (INR) was 1.16
partial thromboplastin time (PTT) was 28 seconds, and anti-Xa levels were less than 0.1
The patient underwent posterior cervical decompression and fusion of C3-T3. The surgical case was completed over the course of two days due to hemodynamic instability during the procedure.
Postoperatively, he remained intubated in the trauma and burn intensive care unit and was successfully extubated three days later.
Due to oropharyngeal dysphagia, he required the placement of a Dobhoff tube and later a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube.
Two months after the injury, the patient was discharged home after a one-month stay in inpatient rehabilitation.
At discharge, he continued to have left-sided weakness and required PEG tube feeding.
the patient had improvement in his left-sided weakness at his outpatient follow-up one month later
